characters: Elorm: 15-year-old Ghanaian boy with a warm, confident smile, wearing a neat navy school polo shirt and glasses, using a digital tablet for communication.
Kobby: 14-year-old Ghanaian boy in the robotics club wearing a cyan robotics club T-shirt, enthusiastic and collaborative.
Robotics Teacher: Supportive Ghanaian STEM teacher in a smart-casual shirt and lanyard.
Technology Entrepreneur: Visiting Ghanaian female tech founder in a tailored jacket.

narrationPlan.voice: Warm, respectful, expressive Ghanaian-English storyteller voice (Kore)
narrationPlan.pace: Steady proficient-reader pace (about 120 words per minute)
notes: Deliver Elorm’s typed tablet lines with wit, intelligence and warmth.
Highlight user co-design, consent/privacy and offline reliability.

music: Innovation Lab Gentle Synth & Piano (warm, modern piano melody ducked beneath narration)
culturalNotes: Elorm (Ewe) and Kobby (Akan diminutive for Kwabena/Kobina) are everyday Ghanaian names whose accurate pronunciation matters in speech technology.
Designing for offline reliability reflects real engineering needs across Ghanaian schools and communities.
reviewQuestions: Does the story show Elorm as intelligent, witty and central to every design decision ("Only if you promise not to make all the decisions for me")?
Are user consent, data privacy, offline fallback reliability and realistic business questions clearly addressed?

pages.brief: 3D animated Ghanaian JHS robotics club room. 15-year-old Elorm in a navy polo shirt and glasses holds a tablet with a warm, witty smile while 14-year-old Kobby in a cyan shirt blushes apologetically beside classmates and robot parts.
pages.narration: Deliver Elorm’s tablet response with dry, confident wit, followed by warm friendliness.

pages.brief: 3D animated robotics club meeting. Kobby and Elorm sit together at a workbench with a laptop and tablet, grinning as they agree to partner on designing an assistive communication tool while their teacher watches approvingly.
pages.narration: Warm, collaborative tone highlighting co-design and mutual respect.

pages.brief: 3D animated robotics lab scene. A tablet screen shows colourful icon buttons while Kobby presses a button and Elorm, Kobby and their teacher laugh good-naturedly at the first prototype test.
pages.narration: Lighthearted classroom laughter and encouraging feedback on iterative prototyping.

pages.brief: 3D animated school studio corner. Elorm and Kobby work with a smiling student volunteer holding a microphone and a consent form, testing Ghanaian name pronunciations carefully on their laptop.
pages.narration: Thoughtful, earnest tone emphasizing why people’s names and representative data matter.

pages.brief: 3D animated robotics club discussion. Elorm looks serious as he shows his tablet to the group, while the teacher explains data privacy and security safeguards to the attentive students.
pages.narration: Serious, reflective tone on Elorm’s question about privacy and consent.

pages.brief: 3D animated school technology exhibition. Kobby looks worried beside a laptop with a disconnected signal icon, while Elorm calmly holds up his tablet displaying an offline visual communication board to applauding visitors.
pages.narration: Build tension when the internet fails, then calm poise from Elorm and warm applause.

pages.brief: 3D animated school innovation hub. A Ghanaian female technology entrepreneur in a smart blazer speaks with Kobby and Elorm beside their prototype table, smiling approvingly at Elorm’s thoughtful response.
pages.narration: Inquisitive, realistic business tone from the entrepreneur and wise restraint from Elorm.

pages.brief: 3D animated classroom demonstration. Elorm sits proudly with his tablet speaking through a clear speaker while Kobby and classmates laugh and cheer warmly around him.
pages.narration: Warm humour on Elorm’s second sentence and a powerful closing distinction between having ideas and expressing them.

pages.brief: 3D animated golden-hour scene in the school robotics room. Kobby and Elorm stand side by side holding an official invitation letter, smiling with quiet determination beside their tablet prototype.
pages.narration: Warm, inspiring conclusion emphasizing that the best inventions begin by listening to people.

teacherGuide.overview: Emphasize that disability does not determine intelligence, personality or ambition. Do not assume that every person with speech difficulties wants the same technology. Learners should explore accessibility through respectful consultation, not by pretending to know another person's lived experience.
learningGoals: Explain how text-to-speech assistive technology works and why co-designing with users is essential.
Identify why representative pronunciation data, informed consent, data privacy and offline reliability matter in responsible software engineering.
Evaluate the practical questions an entrepreneur must research (user needs, maintenance, cost, privacy, affordability) before launching a product.

beforeReading: Discuss the different ways people communicate every day (speech, writing, sign language, gestures, communication boards and text-to-speech tablets).
whileReading: Pause at Page 1 and discuss Elorm’s response ("Of course I can. I am standing right here.") and why we should always speak directly and respectfully to people.
Pause at Page 4 for the quick question on why the app mispronounced some Ghanaian names.
afterReading: Complete the six end-of-story activities covering text-to-speech, user co-design, voice privacy/consent, offline reliability, founder research questions, and sketching an accessible school app feature.
discussion: What did Kobby and Elorm mean when they said, "The technology did not give you ideas... It helps me express them"?
Why was preparing an offline communication board just as important as the software demonstration?
reflection: How can your school or classroom make everyday activities more welcoming and accessible for learners with different needs?

mathsExtension.task: Suppose the robotics club tests 80 Ghanaian names in Prototype 1 and 52 are pronounced accurately. In Prototype 2, after adding volunteer recordings with permission, 74 out of 80 are pronounced accurately. By how many percentage points did accuracy improve?

support: Have learners design a 6-button paper communication board with everyday classroom phrases that works without electricity or internet.
stretch: Have learners write a short privacy and consent checklist that a student technology club must follow before recording voice samples.

culturalNotes: Respecting the accurate pronunciation of Ghanaian names across Akan, Ewe, Ga, Dagbani and other languages is an important part of inclusive technology.
localiseThis: Encourage learners to test how standard devices pronounce names from their own community and discuss why diverse linguistic data matters.

investigation.title: Accessible Offline Communication Board & App Feature Sketch
steps: Identify one everyday school situation where clear, accessible communication helps everyone.
Sketch an app screen or offline communication board with large, clear buttons and respectful phrases.
Write two sentences explaining how your design protects user privacy and works when the internet is offline.
investigation.whatToNotice: Good assistive design combines clear usability, offline reliability and respect for the user’s autonomy.
investigation.safetyNote: Emphasize respectful consultation; never record anyone’s voice or personal data without explicit permission.

reviewerNotes: Confirm open vowel quality (ɔ) without rhotic r.
